rows.what the ink shows: A leading d has a visible left bowl and upright; a final short t-stem rises above the cancellation. The thick double cancellation covers the two intervening letters, so on remains uncertain.
Above the cancelled word are a small closed o, a separate low u-stroke, and a short grave accent above its right half. The replacement is physically above the deletion.

A long cancellation obliterates the baseline between élément and the following u. Two isolated upright remnants and a final high hook remain, but they do not distinguish the original words or symbols.

The cancelled line has distinct x, membership strokes, E, comma, then a descending y, membership strokes, F and comma. Before x is an additional looped angled glyph, plausibly a quantifier or Si, whose dense overstroke prevents a secure reading.

After the two baseline norm factors, a raised character has the curved head, descending diagonal and short foot of 2. Its height is above the final baseline bars; the adjoining rightward curl belongs to the cancellation.
Inside the citation parentheses the digit has an open angled left arm and a right descending stem. There is no closed lower loop of 6.

The cancelled lower line has a b-like ascender in the first long word and a descending f-like stroke in the following word; the middle is heavily overwritten. A small looped d followed by low an/s strokes is clear immediately before the tensor-product formula; extra upper-line strokes cannot be securely assigned to the proposed phrase.

After the canceled “En effet,” the horizontal deletion buries nearly the entire baseline; a few low blobs and an x-like crossed remnant at the right survive, but no complete letter sequence is recoverable. No distinct raised letter or index can be isolated.

The uncanceled word above the deleted line begins with a broad low m, followed by separated low round/linear strokes and a taller hooked t; the final low strokes fit r-ons. It lies immediately before the clear “que l’espace” continuation.

The lower canceled line preserves an initial loop and upright of “et” and the looped l plus e-s of “les”. The higher continuation has a round opening, several short internal strokes and a tall final-word loop, but the sloping cancellation covers enough of both word baselines that “combinaisons finies” cannot be fully distinguished.

The later loop has its long descender on the left and a rounded body to the right, favoring q and a following low ue; the same-page q of “que l’espace” likewise carries a long left descender. No separate tall t is visible in this ending, so “suite” is less supported, but the crossed middle and interval before q still prevent certifying the whole word “puisque”.
The opening r and a small raised acute mark are followed by a low joined sequence, a taller l and the short terminal t-e strokes. The word ends before the visibly separate “en effet”.

The canceled phrase retains four word onsets: the tall opening l, a small c, the rounded rising d of the third word and the long looped f of “forme”. The remaining low joins lie along the deletion stroke; no extra tall letter appears inside the final word.

After “forme”, a short vertical stroke and low arc remain, followed by a heavily retraced central blot and two isolated rising/falling strokes toward the right. The cancellation hides the internal letters and word divisions, so no complete sequence or raised glyph is securely readable.
